brief.text:
The clearest signal in today's data is security risk around Gulf oil infrastructure and the Strait of Hormuz. MarineLink reports that Yemen's Houthis say they struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the kingdom's biggest, with a ballistic missile. Separately, Seatrade Maritime reports Iran's Hormuz authority (PGSA) will take "legal action" from 1 November against the Sinokor fleet, claiming its vessels breached transit rules for the strait. For anyone fixing ships, both items sit on the same loading region, so expect owners and charterers to be asking about war-risk cover and transit terms before they commit tonnage.

On prices, the only fresh moves are bunkers — the fuel ships burn — and the Baltic Dry Index. VLSFO (very low sulphur fuel oil, the standard 0.5% sulphur marine fuel) rose at all four hubs: Houston 843.00 USD/t, up 26.00 (+3.2%); Singapore 980.00 USD/t, up 17.00 (+1.8%); Fujairah 989.50 USD/t, up 8.50 (+0.9%); Rotterdam 772.00 USD/t, up 6.00 (+0.8%). The data here does not show why; the Ras Tanura headline is one possible factor for the Gulf and Asian hubs, but nothing in the data confirms it, and Houston moved most. The Baltic Dry Index, which tracks dry bulk freight, fell 25.00 points to 2,603.00 (-1.0%), with no headline here explaining it. Brent (109.19), WTI (101.34), the Brent-WTI spread (7.85) and RBOB gasoline (3.05) are all marked stale and are not today's figures, so treat them as unavailable. We have no freight route rates at all — no TCE (time charter equivalent, the daily earnings figure a voyage converts to) for any vessel class.

This is the first brief, so nothing is carried forward. Opening today: the Houthi strike; the PGSA–Sinokor dispute; QatarEnergy extending force majeure on Adriatic LNG cargoes to Edison until end-December; Russia's claim that Northern Sea Route transit cargo will nearly double in 2026; and International Seaways expanding its VLCC fleet (VLCC = very large crude carrier, roughly two million barrels) through a "strategic combination".

Watch two things. First, whether bunker premiums at Fujairah and Singapore hold or widen against Rotterdam, since that spread is where Gulf disruption would show up in the fuel you stem. Second, 1 November, when PGSA says its action against Sinokor begins — that is a dated, checkable event rather than a rumour.
